title: aki vs. amely: People and Things

sections.content: You know *aki* from A2 Unit 4. This lesson adds *amely*, its partner for things. This lesson is about a document, the Golden Bull, so you need a relative pronoun for things as well as people. Hungarian keeps these strictly separate: *aki* only ever refers to a person, while *amely* (and its plural *amelyek*) refers back to a thing, a document, an institution or any other non-person noun that was already named. A closely related word, *ami*, is used instead of *amely* when there's no specific earlier noun to point back to (roughly "what" or "whatever") — *amely* is the one you'll need most for referring to something specific, like a named law.

sections.title: Choosing the right relative pronoun
rows: which, that (a specific thing already named — a law, a document, an institution)
what, that (general or indefinite reference, no specific antecedent)

items.spanish: II. András, aki 1222-ben kiadta az Aranybullát, engedett a nemesség nyomásának.
items.english: Andrew II, who issued the Golden Bull in 1222, gave in to the nobility's pressure.

items.spanish: Az Aranybullát, amely korlátozta a király hatalmát, sokan az angol Magna Chartával hasonlítják össze.
items.english: Many people compare the Golden Bull, which limited the king's power, with England's Magna Carta.

items.spanish: A törvény, amely az ellenállás jogát is biztosította, a király hatalmát korlátozta.
items.english: The law, which also guaranteed the right of resistance, limited the king's power.

sections.content: A common mistake at this level is using *aki* for a document or institution, on the model of English "the law who...". Always ask first: is the antecedent a person, or a thing? *II. András* is a person → *aki*. *Az Aranybulla* is a document → *amely*. Once you have the two pronouns straight, you can describe a whole event in one sentence: who did it (*aki*), and what it produced (*amely*).
